I'm the fractional chief AI officer your org chart can point at when a customer asks who owns AI risk. I set up the governance an enterprise security review asks for, then get one process live for real users, with evals, tracing, a rollback path and a cost per outcome.
Three or more of these five signs? You're exactly who this is for.

/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-.text: What actually belongs in an AI acceptable use policy — meshin.co

An AI acceptable use policy only earns its place once it decides who approves a new AI tool and which data tier may reach which category of vendor. It also decides whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer or a contract, and when a customer must be told they are dealing with an

By the time a policy is drafted, some staff are already using AI without asking anyone first. That means drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account, running a browser extension nobody vetted, or building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves. That is shadow AI, and treat

The same person who is already accountable for AI risk generally should hold this document. A shared inbox cannot hold it, because someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed o

The version I run for my own practice is public at my AI policy, one page, as a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The Starter Kit sets out the same structure as a table you can copy, sized for a company with more than one person to coordinate.

A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, that gap usually surfaces during an AI readiness and risk assessment before it ever reaches the policy stage, because there is no obvious person to hand the draft to.

/blog/category/agentic-architecture.text: An agent demo is easy and an agent in production is not, and the gap between them is almost never about the model. It is about the same engineering discipline any other system needs, applied to a component whose output is not deterministic.

Start with evaluation, before the prompt. You need to say what a good answer looks like on a set of real cases. Otherwise you cannot tell whether a change made the system better or simply different. Build the eval set from work people have already done, so there is a known-good answer to compare aga

Put that eval run in continuous integration. This is the single change that most often turns a prototype into something a team will let near a customer. It moves the question from an argument about vibes to a number that blocks a merge. A regression should fail the build, in the same job, with the s

Instrument every call. When an answer is wrong you want to see which retrieval returned which document and what the model was given, not reconstruct it from memory. Tracing turns a support escalation into a quick check instead of a day of guessing.

Set a cost ceiling per outcome and check it in the same job as the evals. A loop that retries three times on a bad tool response is fine in a demo and ruinous at volume. If you cannot state the cost of one completed task, you do not yet know whether the system makes sense.

Then design the boundary. Tool interfaces are where agents actually break. That is why an explicit protocol between the model and your systems is worth adopting, rather than one improvised inside a prompt. Keep the tools narrow, validate their inputs, and make every destructive action reversible.
Finally, keep a rollback path. A prompt is a deployment. Version it, ship it behind the same controls as code, and be able to put yesterday back quickly.

/blog/category/executive.text: A board does not need a member who can explain how a model works. It needs to know who inside the company is answerable when one gets something wrong in front of a customer. It also needs to know whether that answer would survive being read back in a dispute. Ask that question at every review, not j

Ask for three things, by name rather than by department. Who owns AI risk, specifically, not which team owns it. A register of every AI system in use, kept current rather than produced once for an audit. And the last time a customer or a regulator asked a question about this, with the answer that wa

Do not ask for a demo. A demo proves a model can perform once, in front of people who want it to succeed, which is the least useful thing a board can learn. Do not ask for a token count, a model name, or a list of pilots. Those measure activity, not risk, and a company can produce an impressive slid

The exposure that actually matters shows up after something goes wrong, not before. A regulator or an insurer will not ask whether the model was good. They will ask whether someone reviewed the system before it reached a customer. They will also ask whether that review is written down, and whether t

A company of 30 to 300 people needs one named owner, one page of decisions, and the discipline to update both when something changes. A board does this well by asking the same few questions until the answers stop moving.

/blog/category/governance.text: Governance has a bad name in small companies because most of what is sold under that name is written for a bank. A three hundred person company does not need a committee, a maturity model or a consultant to run a workshop. It needs four things that fit on a shared drive and get updated when somethin

The first is a register: every AI system in use, who owns it, what data reaches it. It also records whether a person checks its output before a customer sees it. Companies usually find more AI in the building than they expected, because someone signed up for a tool with a credit card and nobody wrot

The second is an acceptable-use policy short enough that people read it. One page. What you may paste into a chat window, what you may not, and who to ask when the answer is unclear. A policy that requires a training course to understand is a policy that gets ignored by the people whose behaviour it

The third is a data classification table. Three or four tiers, each with a rule about which vendors may see that tier. This is the document that answers most of a customer security questionnaire. It is also the one companies most often skip, because it requires a decision rather than a description.

The fourth is a named owner: one person whose job description says they own AI risk and who has the authority to stop a launch. That is the whole set. It takes about two weeks to produce honestly, and the honest version is worth more than a thorough version that describes a company you are not. /blog/category/operating-model.text: Most stalled AI programmes are not blocked on technology. They are blocked because nobody can say who decides whether a system is allowed to touch customer data. Nobody owns the outcome once the pilot team moves on, either.

An operating model answers three questions. Who chooses which processes get automated. Who reviews a system before it reaches a customer. Who runs it afterwards. If the answer to any of those is a team name rather than a person, the work will drift until someone senior gets nervous and stops it.

Choice comes first, and it is mostly a filter. A candidate process needs volume, a measurable outcome, and a tolerable failure mode. Volume, because a system used twice a week never accumulates enough signal to improve. A measurable outcome, because a metric you have to survey for cannot gate a rele

Review comes second. It should be boring and written down: what evidence a launch needs, who signs, and what evidence would stop it. In practice this is a short checklist attached to the register entry, not a governance ceremony. The point is that the answer exists before someone needs it at eleven

Ownership comes third and is the one that gets skipped. A pilot that reaches production without a named internal owner becomes shadow infrastructure: nobody updates it, nobody watches its cost, and its failure surprises everyone. Handover is a deliverable, not a formality, and it only counts once so

This is also why fractional works for companies of this size. You need the decisions made properly once, written down, and handed to someone inside the company. You do not need a permanent executive to maintain four documents and a review checklist. An engagement that does not end has usually replac

The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one, and a model provider’s silent update slips through every time. A working entry names what the system does, what data can reach it, which vendor or model sits behind it, who owns it, and a rough risk tier. Some call this same list an AI register rather than an AI system register. Most of the systems on it never started as a formal AI project, which is why the li

The NIST AI RMF treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry.

The registration duty in the EU AI Act is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that sepa

If you would rather someone else run the discovery and the first risk pass, an AI Readiness & Risk Assessment does the same work in two weeks and hands you a finished register. The starter kit has a blank version of this table, ready to copy into your own document.

One named person, not a shared folder. They do not need to personally approve every new AI tool. But they need standing to ask why an unlisted system turned up, and a fixed date on the calendar to confirm every row is still accurate.

/glossary/ai-management-system.text: What is an AI management system? — meshin.co

The EU AI Act does not require this broader system. Article 17 requires a narrower relative of it instead. Every provider of a high-risk AI system must run a documented quality management system, covering the risk-management process, post-market monitoring and serious-incident procedures among other

Set a fixed date to review the register rather than waiting for a customer to ask. I score exactly this structure against ISO/IEC 42001 in the two-week AI readiness and risk assessment, so the gap list is evidence rather than a guess.

/glossary/ai-register.text: What is an AI register? — meshin.co
An AI register is a company's own inventory of every AI system it builds, buys or uses, listing what it does, what data it touches, who owns it and how risky it is.

The honest answer to "what AI do you run" is too often "we are not sure." Building a register does not need new software. It forces one decision per system: a named owner. That turns a question a reviewer might spend a day chasing into a document you hand over in a meeting.

/glossary/conformity-assessment.text: What is a conformity assessment? — meshin.co

A conformity assessment is the process a provider completes before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, either checking it internally or having an accredited outside body check it. It shows the system actually meets the EU AI Act's requirements, rather than merely claiming to.

For almost every high-risk system, the outcome is simple: the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off inste

Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standard

Work out early, before the system is built, which assessment route applies, since a notified-body review takes far longer to arrange than an internal one and cannot be rushed at launch. Keep the assessment evidence alongside the technical documentation it depends on, not in a file only one person ca

/glossary/data-classification.text: NIST's own method for federal systems ties each category to a real question, not a subjective label: what actually happens to confidentiality, integrity or availability if this breaks? That means naming who could see this data, alter it, or take it offline. A scheme built the same way works for

Keep the scheme small. Three or four tiers is enough for most companies, and a scheme nobody can remember gets ignored the same as none. Map every AI tool in the register to which tiers may reach it. Make the most important rule explicit: customer data and secrets never go into an unclassified tool.

/glossary/dpia.text: Write the DPIA before the system is built, not after, since a risk found during design is cheap to change and the same risk found after launch usually is not. Start from what is actually being collected and why, not from a template’s headings, and consult the data protection officer while there is t

/glossary/eu-ai-act.text: What is the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there. That is why a US-based star

In practice, it changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight, with evidence of both ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

/glossary/evals.text: Evals are repeatable tests that score an AI system's outputs against a fixed set of examples and criteria, run before release and again whenever the prompt, data or model changes.

Engineering teams build them because "it worked when I tried it a few times" does not survive a prompt change six months later, once nobody remembers which cases mattered. Security reviewers and boards ask about them because an eval suite is the concrete answer to "how do you know it

/glossary/guardrails.text: What are guardrails in an AI system? — meshin.co

Guardrails are the checks placed around what an AI model can be asked, what it can say, and what it can do. They are enforced in the surrounding code, not left to the model's training. That way an unusual input cannot simply talk the system out of a rule.

This is closer to what NIST's AI Risk Management Framework calls its Manage function: turning a risk decision into something the system enforces, not something merely written down. Guardrails are how that function shows up in code, not in a policy document nobody checks against production.

Write guardrails as rules the code enforces, not text pasted into a prompt. Test each one against an input designed to defeat it, not a well-behaved example. Put a real check in front of any action that spends money, changes a record, or sends something external. That way a failure blocks the action

/glossary/hallucination-rate.text: What is a hallucination rate? — meshin.co
A hallucination rate is the share of a model's answers that state something false or invented in the same confident tone as a correct one, measured against questions with known correct answers.

NIST's generative-AI risk guidance calls this failure confabulation, distinct from an ordinary software bug because confidence is never a reliable guide to accuracy here. That makes it different from a crash or an error message, which at least announces itself. A model rarely answers "I don

Measure the rate on the eval suite’s real cases, not a generic public benchmark. Behaviour on general trivia says little about a specific product’s actual questions. Track the number after every prompt or model change, the way an eval pass rate is tracked. Do not measure it once and assume it holds.

/glossary/high-risk-ai-system.text: What makes an AI system high-risk? — meshin.co

A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of, or itself, a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, such as medical devices or machinery. That underlying law already requires third-party conformity assessment.

Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk for landing in one of those areas alone, with no product-safety law involved at all.

A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task: reformatting an application into a standard template, say. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing i

A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at t

Run the classification test on each system separately, not on the company as a whole. One product can be high-risk while another, built the same month, is not. Write the decision down, including the reasoning for a not-high-risk conclusion, since an authority can ask to see it later. This classifica

/glossary/human-in-the-loop.text: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or can stop an AI system's output before it takes effect, rather than the system acting on its own once it starts.

Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. It is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about, for anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing.

Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and

/glossary/human-oversight.text: What does human oversight require under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

Article 14 spells out five specific capacities the overseeing person needs. They must understand the system's real limits well enough to spot a malfunction, and stay alert to automation bias rather than trusting the output by default. They also need to correctly read what the output actually mea

Name the specific person or role authorised to halt each high-risk system, not a team, and check they have time per case to evaluate output rather than approve on reflex. Train that person specifically on automation bias. A rushed or over-trusting reviewer defeats the requirement even when the proce

/glossary/iso-iec-42001.text: ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence published it in December 2023. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act stru

Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard a company can be audited and certified against by an accredited third party. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask where you sit against it, because certification gives them a documented, externally checked

Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. Through that point, a company can control who is allowed to call a model. It can log every prompt and response for an audit trail, and redact sensitive data before it leaves the b

/glossary/model-card.text: What is a model card? — meshin.co

A model card is a short, standard-shaped document a model's maker publishes. It describes what the model was built for, and how it performs across groups and conditions. It also names where the model should not be used, closer to a spec sheet than a sales page.

NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a

Ask every model vendor for their card before signing. Read the limitations section before the headline numbers: the numbers are chosen by the vendor, and the limitations rarely are. If a company fine-tunes or wraps a base model itself, write a short card of its own. Describe what changed and what wa

That distinction decides who actually reads the summary, and when: before a contract is signed, not after a customer's legal team

Ask every model vendor what the model was trained on, or where its training-data summary sits if the vendor owes one. Ask what licence covers the weights and output. Record the answer in the AI register next to that system, not in an email thread nobody can find during a review. Reading the actual v

/glossary/nist-ai-rmf.text: What is the NIST AI RMF? — meshin.co
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is a voluntary US framework, published in January 2023, for identifying and managing an AI system's risks across its design, development and use.

The framework sets out four functions an organisation applies to an AI system. GOVERN covers policy and accountability, while MAP covers understanding context and risk. Testing and metrics fall under MEASURE. Acting on what it found is MANAGE's job.

It is not a law, and it is not sector specific. A bank, a hospital and a ten-person startup can all use the same structure. US procurement teams, and increasingly non-US ones, ask about it because it gives a common vocabulary for a question that used to have no fixed answer. That question is how you

/glossary/observability.text: What is observability for an AI system? — meshin.co

Observability is the ability to see, after the fact, exactly what a live AI system was asked. For any one case someone points to, it also shows what the system retrieved or called, and what it answered. An aggregate chart alone cannot explain one specific customer's bad experience.

This differs from a simple uptime dashboard. It can show a system is running while saying nothing about whether one specific answer, given to one specific person, was actually right. NIST's risk management framework calls this its Measure function: a system only counts as measured if it keeps be

Log the full input, every step the system took including tool calls, and the output for every real request, not a sample. Keep those logs long enough to support an investigation. Make sure any one case can be pulled up by its own reference, rather than only appearing inside an average. This logging,

/glossary/post-market-monitoring.text: What is post-market monitoring under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

The monitoring plan is not a separate document. Article 72 makes it part of the system's technical documentation, built and updated alongside it, not bolted on after a complaint. A pattern the monitoring turns up is also the raw material for the next duty in the chain: deciding whether what happ

A monitoring system that never hears from the people using it day to day is monitoring very little. The Fractional CAIO Retainer I run keeps this review on a fixed schedule, not only when a customer complains.

/glossary/prompt-injection.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is sc

Never let a model’s output directly trigger a sensitive action without a check enforced in code. Keep the model’s own permissions to the smallest set it needs. Treat anything the model reads from outside the conversation as untrusted input, the way a web application treats a user-supplied string. Ev

/glossary/provider-vs-deployer.text: What is the difference between a provider and a deployer? — meshin.co
Provider vs deployer is the EU AI Act split between the company that builds an AI system and the company that runs it. Most of the Act's paperwork depends on which of the two roles a company holds.

Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. Giving the system away under your o

A deployer is defined by use, not branding: using the system under the deployer's own authority. The only carve-out is personal, non-professional activity. A company using a tool internally is a deployer even if it never touches a customer.

That test has a sharp edge. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the com

Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company. Rebranding one vendor’s model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. The duty falls on the provider, the company that built the system, and sometimes on the deployer, the company running it. It applies once a malfunction leads to death, serious harm, or a serious breach of someone's fundamental rights.

Once the report is filed, the provider has to investigate: assess the risk, take corrective action, and cooperate with the authority. It cannot alter the system in a way that would affect the investigation's findings without telling the authority first. The duty also covers serious harm to prope

Decide in advance, in writing, who has the authority to judge that an incident is serious enough to report, rather than leaving that call to whoever notices the problem first. /glossary/shadow-ai.text: Shadow AI is any AI tool an employee uses for company work without IT or security's knowledge. Examples range from a personal chatbot account to a browser extension or a locally run model.

The hardest form to spot is a model downloaded and run locally on a laptop. It never crosses the network as a request to a known AI vendor. The same problem shows up wherever an employee reaches for a tool without asking. A developer might call a model's API directly from a side project. A brows

/glossary/sub-processor.text: A sub-processor is a vendor an AI provider hands a company's data to behind the scenes. The model provider behind a SaaS tool is a common example. GDPR Article 28 requires the provider to get the customer's permission, and to bind the sub-processor to the same data protections by contract.

The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops

Ask every AI vendor for its sub-processor list, and how it notifies customers of a change. Then check honestly: does the notice give a real chance to object, or just a record that it happened? /resources/agent-evals-ci-starter.text: A CI workflow and an eval case format for one agentic workflow. The same discipline sits inside the 90-Day Production Sprint. A prompt or model change should not merge without passing a test set first.

The tags borrow their shape from OWASP’s Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications. Prompt injection and excessive agency (the agent doing something nobody asked it to) show up in a support agent as often as in a public chatbot. A tagged case catches the regression either way.

It is not a considered eval set on its own. A handful of cases pulled from real conversations tests more than a long list invented at a desk. The starter takes no position on which cases you pick, and that part still maps to the MEASURE function (one of the framework’s four functions) in NIST’s AI R

/resources/ai-readiness-scorecard.text: Copy the table into a spreadsheet or your own wiki. Score each axis yourself, or better, ask three people to score it separately and compare notes. A gap between an engineer's score and a board member's score is often more telling than the total.

Five axes, scored from zero to three, that give you a rough position before you pay anyone to check it properly. The axes match the ones in the AI Readiness & Risk Assessment. This is the self-administered version, without the evidence behind it.
The five axes are not a substitute for the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) or ISO/IEC 42001. They are a rougher pass at the same territory, built to take an afternoon rather than an audit.

/resources/build-vs-buy-ai-kit.text: Build vs Buy AI Kit — meshin.co
Weight the six criteria for your situation, score build and buy against each one, and let the total argue with your gut feeling. A bought tool still needs an owner and a place in your AI register.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) treats a vendor’s model the same as one you trained, under its MAP function (one of the framework’s four functions). The risk to your customer does not care who wrote the code.

It is not a procurement process, and it will not pick the vendor for you. It decides one thing: whether the job belongs inside your codebase or inside someone else’s product. /resources/llm-gateway-governance-config.text: A policy file for whichever LLM gateway you run, hosted or self-built. It is the config, not the gateway itself. The decisions live in a file your team reviews, not in a script only one engineer remembers.

The logging schema borrows its shape from the EU AI Act’s Article 12, which requires automatic event logs for high-risk systems. Not every call through a gateway is high-risk. The habit costs little to build in now. It is expensive to retrofit once a regulator or a customer asks first.

The allowed_models and log_retention keys map to two NIST SP 800-53 control families: Access Control and Audit and Accountability. A procurement questionnaire is often built from this catalogue, even when nobody names it.

It is not a gateway, and it will not stop a determined engineer from calling a model directly. It makes an unrouted call a shadow AI finding. That is the layer the 90-Day Production Sprint puts in front of a workflow before it counts as production.
